editorNote: Holiday disks offer world conquest, mysterious systems and a voyage among the planets.
morningLine: At the game counter, a whole world fits on a 48K disk.

lead.headline: Atari holiday shelf offers worlds to conquer
body: A home computer can become a council of world powers, an Eastern Front battlefield or an unexplained terminal this holiday season. November’s Antic product notices offer Atari owners a broad choice of disk adventures. These are the month’s listed offerings, not a fresh batch of releases dated to Thanksgiving week.

SSI lists Colonial Conquest at $39.95 for a 48K Atari disk system. Up to six players represent Germany, France, England, Japan, Russia and the United States in a nineteenth-century contest for world power. For a smaller-scale military problem, Roger Damon’s Panzer Grenadier, also $39.95, moves German and Russian platoons and companies across the Second World War’s Eastern Front.

Activision takes a different approach with Hacker. The $24.95, 48K disk title casts the player into a mysterious computer-system simulation. It is entertainment built around investigation, not a tool for breaking into a real machine. Mindscape’s $44.95 Halley Project, from Tom Snyder Productions, sends the player through solar-system navigation tests in a real-time simulation.

There is reading as well as maneuvering on the shelf. Synapse’s Brimstone, distributed by Broderbund, is listed as a $35.95 medieval electronic novel; the notice specifies 48K and two disk drives. The buying lesson is to check the equipment list as carefully as the title. Antic’s manufacturer-supplied notices are introductions to products, not independent tests of their performance.

stories.headline: Windows faces the holiday buying test
body: Microsoft’s newly shipped Windows reaches the holiday shopping season with a $99 software price and a visual alternative to the DOS command line. Shipment took place November 20, before this issue’s week, after a wait stretching back to the 1983 announcement. The question now is what PC owners can do with it.

Windows runs above DOS rather than replacing it. Tiled application windows, menus and a mouse-oriented interface organize the screen, while Write, Paint, Notepad, Calendar, Clock, Cardfile, Terminal and a file manager provide practical work. Reversi supplies a little recreation between tasks.

Those included programs make the package tangible, but they are not evidence of a mature outside software market. A buyer is choosing an operating environment for an existing PC, with the machine and DOS still part of the bill. The holiday verdict belongs to users, not predictions about the platform’s distant future.

stories.headline: Trackstar offers a second life for Apple disks
body: A $499 expansion board offers IBM PC owners an unusual way to keep older software useful. Russ Lockwood’s November Creative Computing review describes Diamond Computer Systems’ Trackstar, with a 6502 for Apple II Plus programs and a Z80A for CP/M software. It can use the PC’s drives and includes a connector for an Apple drive.

Compatibility is the important qualification. Almost all educational titles tested worked, but only about half the games did; software written specifically for the Apple IIe did not run. The prudent purchase starts with a trial of the actual programs the owner wants to preserve, not a blanket promise that every disk will cross the divide.

stories.headline: MPP lives on under Supra
body: Atari owners looking for Microbits service have a new name to remember. Gigi Bisson’s November Antic report says Alan Ackerman and John Wiley’s Supra bought the Microbits name on July 1, after the bank closed MPP at the end of May. This is current-month reporting of an earlier rescue, not a new acquisition this week.

Supra honors the 90-day warranty on products sold after July 1; earlier purchases may carry $15 to $35 handling charges. Orders were being accepted for the plug-in MPP 1200A modem and MicroNet, which allows as many as eight Ataris to share drives and printers. The announced $800, 10MB hard disk remains delayed rather than a shipping product.

briefs.headline: The Source steps up to 2400 baud
briefs.summary: November Antic lists access at 46 cents per minute during weekday prime time and 20 cents off-peak. Faster access does not make the clock stop charging.

briefs.headline: Rocky IV tops the Thanksgiving screen
briefs.summary: The November 29-December 1 US weekend brings Rocky IV $19,991,537 and first place. Its November 27 opening falls within this issue week.

periodAd.headline: A picture through the joystick port
periodAd.summary: Digital Vision lists Computereyes at $129.95 for the interface and software, or $399.95 with a monochrome camera. Slow-scan black-and-white images can be saved in KoalaPad-compatible files.
periodAd.tagline: Editorial reconstruction of manufacturer notice, not a tested endorsement.

market.headline: Expansion versus replacement
market.summary: Trackstar asks $499 to carry selected Apple II Plus and CP/M software into a PC. RAM 7 lists 256K at $195 or 384K at $225. Compatibility limits and the software already owned matter as much as the sticker.

worldAnchor.headline: Atlantis launches with three communications satellites
worldAnchor.summary: Atlantis launched November 26 at 7:29 p.m. EST on STS-61B with seven crew members, including Mexico’s Rodolfo Neri Vela. Its payloads include MORELOS-B, AUSSAT-2 and SATCOM KU-2, alongside EASE/ACCESS construction experiments.

bbsNote.headline: Faster paid services, and Atari conversations without a phone bill
bbsNote.summary: November Antic supplies real service rates and a ham-radio alternative. These are period editorial desk notes, not actual recovered BBS posts.

posts.text: Service advertised online at 2400 baud; 46 cents per minute prime time and 20 cents off-peak.

Marquardt reports regular Atari 800 RTTY exchanges with Larry Johnson (WB6SVS) and a direct range beyond 100 miles, without telephone charges. MFJ-1224 costs $99.95; Hamtext $99.95 adds disk-buffer facilities.
MPP 1200A orders were being accepted; do not invent a price or shipment date.

curiosity.headline: Your Atari can guard the windows
curiosity.summary: Two November product notices turn the joystick port into a home-security interface.
curiosity.detail: C.E.A. Home Control is listed at $89.95 with four-device control, a power module and temperature control; Hard Byte Security is $99.95 and includes three window sensors, 30 feet of glass foil and a door sensor. These are manufacturer notices, not tested security guarantees.

undergroundDesk.headline: Phrack travels from board to board
undergroundDesk.dek: A November electronic newsletter introduces a publishing circle at Metal Shop.
body: The first Phrack issue, dated November 17, introduces a newsletter-like collection of eight files. Taran King identifies Metal Shop as its home board and invites writers to contribute and other boards to redistribute the files. Its appearance precedes this issue week; the story is its same-month arrival in bulletin-board culture.

The introduction names contributors including Knight Lightning and Cheap Shades. Its self-described interests span hacking, phone phreaking and cracking, but the publishing network is the news here: a collection can travel without a press or a paper subscription. No technical procedures or dial-in details are reproduced.
